title: Alliance for the Wild Rockies and Local Residents Halt Northern Idaho Logging Project in Old Growth Forest and Grizzly Bear Habitat
author: Mike Garrity
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/idahogarrity-680x462.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/21/alliance-
for-the-wild-rockies-and-local-residents-halt-northern-idaho-logging-project-
in-old-growth-forest-and-grizzly-bear-habitat/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/idahogarrity-680x462.png)

Hanna Flats, Idaho Panhandle National Forest. Photo: Paul Sieracki.

Seven long years ago the Alliance for the Wild Rockies, with the support of
local residents, took the Forest Service to federal court to halt the Hanna
Flats logging, road-building, and burning project on the Idaho Panhandle
National Forest. Through a long and winding legal saga the good news -- for
grizzly bears, old growth forests, and the local populace which strongly
opposed the deforestation -- is that the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals just
ruled for the Alliance, halting the project and requiring the Forest Service
to follow the law as written, not the agency's arbitrary interpretation.

The project, supposedly to reduce wildfire risk, is located in the habitat of
the imperiled Selkirk grizzly bears, which are in dire straits having been
reduced to a mere 50 bears when the minimum needed for recovery is 100 bears.
The bears suffer from human-caused mortality at unsustainable rates and are
regularly displaced and harmed from logging and road-building in their
habitat.

Ignoring the fact that grizzly bears are protected by the Endangered Species
Act, the Forest Service authorized 2,203 acres of logging, 139 acres of
burning, and incorporated 30.4 miles of illegally-constructed roads the agency
classified as "temporary" and intended to use for logging roads.

The agency then used what the Court found to be an illegal definition of the
Wildland Urban Interface to claim the project was "categorically excluded"
from conducting an environmental assessment and providing the public the
opportunity for review, comment, and objection.

Contrary to Forest Service claims that the logging was necessary to protect
communities from wildfire, the upper Priest River area's bowl-shaped
topography captures cold air in the low elevations and traps cool moist air in
the summer. The low elevation winter snowpack is deeper and more persistent
than elsewhere in northern Idaho, and summertime conditions are relatively
moist and cool compared to neighboring areas. Hence, the area is not as
susceptible to wildfires.

The Court found that the Forest Service had used a “key assumption” that the
Project is located within a wildland-urban interface but improperly applied
Bonner County’s definition of a wildland-urban interface, which is a broader
definition unmoored from the specifics of the Healthy Forests Restoration
Act."

This is a big win for endangered grizzly bears, but in addition to protecting
the grizzly bears, the Court's ruling also protects the rights of the
homeowners in this area who strongly opposed the massive clearcutting
operations that would destroy the forests around their homes and trails and
lead to harmful sedimentation of rivers and streams. Throughout the years of
litigation, the local residents bravely stood up and spoke truth to power to
protect their home. There is no doubt that their resistance and strength
helped bring about this victory.

There is really no hope of recovering this imperiled grizzly population as
required by the Endangered Species Act unless the government starts complying
with the law. This court decision is one step in the right direction — clearly
demanding that government agencies must follow the law just like everyone
else.

The fight to save our forests and grizzly bears is not over, however, since
the Appeals Court sent the case back to the federal district court of Idaho
for further review. It is not easy to fight the federal government, especially
under Trump, but the Alliance wins 80% of our lawsuits and we need your help
to keep winning, keep our forests standing and our wildlife from going
extinct. This victory is even more important since the Trump administration
declared the federal government no longer has to protect habitat for
threatened and endangered species.
